title: Expression Interpretation and LLVM Compilation
subtitle: Evaluate one typed expression tree two ways: recursively in C++ and as optimized native code generated through LLVM.
assignment_brief: Implement constants, indexed arguments, explicit casts, and binary arithmetic over signed 64-bit integers and doubles.
Every expression supports two execution paths. evaluate recursively interprets the tree and returns an opaque 64-bit payload; build recursively emits typed LLVM IR for the same semantics.

ExpressionCompiler wraps the generated tree in a function with the raw ABI data64_t compiled_expression(data64_t* args), hands the module to the LLVM ORC JIT, resolves the machine-code address, and executes it.
learning_outcomes: Trace one expression tree through both recursive interpretation and recursive LLVM construction.
Explain why data64_t is a transport container for bits rather than the semantic numeric type.
Distinguish a representation-preserving bitcast from a value-changing numeric cast.
Select typed LLVM instructions for integer and floating arithmetic, including signed integer division.
Reconstruct a formula from SSA definitions and constant-fold it when inputs become compile-time constants.
State the generated function ABI and the lifetime requirements of its module, JIT, context, arguments, and function pointer.
Interpret the benchmark as steady-state execution cost only, and identify the operations and edge cases it does not measure.
artifacts: include/moderndbs/codegen/expression.h expression hierarchy and compiler interface
include/moderndbs/codegen/jit.h and src/codegen/jit.cc ORC JIT wrapper

concepts.title: One tree, two execution strategies
concepts.takeaway: The interpreter computes now; the compiler constructs a typed program that computes later.
explanation: evaluate walks the expression tree at runtime. A binary node recursively evaluates its children, decodes their raw payloads according to the node's ValueType, performs the C++ operation, and re-encodes the result.

build performs the same structural recursion but returns llvm::Value objects. It emits IR nodes such as add or fadd instead of calculating the answer. ExpressionCompiler supplies the function and entry block around the recursively generated body.
pseudocode: if leaf: decode/load and return raw result bits
recursively build typed child llvm::Value objects
invariants: Both children of a binary node have the same semantic ValueType.
Interpreter and compiled paths implement the same value semantics for defined inputs.
The expression objects must outlive interpretation or compilation because parents store child references.
pitfalls: Computing a value inside build instead of emitting IR.
Choosing an integer LLVM instruction for a DOUBLE node or an FP instruction for INT64.
Assuming the raw uint64_t payload itself determines the semantic type.

concepts.title: Opaque data64_t transport and the generated ABI
concepts.takeaway: Every argument and result crosses the C++/JIT boundary as exactly 64 raw bits; ValueType tells the code how to interpret those bits.
explanation: data64_t is uint64_t because signed integers and IEEE doubles are both eight bytes. An integer payload contains the two's-complement bits of int64_t; a double payload contains the double's IEEE representation.

The generated function has the ABI i64 compiled_expression(ptr args). INT64 Argument nodes load i64. DOUBLE Argument nodes load double from the corresponding eight-byte slot. A DOUBLE root is bitcast to i64 before return so the external function signature remains uniform.
pseudocode: INT64 argument: load i64 from slot[index]
DOUBLE argument: load double from the same eight-byte slot[index]
DOUBLE result: bitcast double -> i64 for transport
caller decodes returned bits using root ValueType
invariants: Each argument slot is exactly eight bytes.
The caller encodes each slot according to the Argument node's declared ValueType.
A DOUBLE result is representation-bitcast, not numerically converted, at the ABI boundary.
pitfalls: Treating the uint64_t decimal value as the represented double.
Passing a null args pointer to an expression that contains Argument nodes.
Reading an argument with a different ValueType than the caller used to encode it.
Using reinterpret_cast lvalue dereferences where std::bit_cast or memcpy would avoid C++ aliasing undefined behavior.

source_refs.note: Declares the opaque eight-byte carrier.
Emits typed loads from eight-byte argument slots.

concepts.title: Numeric conversion is not bit reinterpretation
concepts.takeaway: Cast changes the numeric value's representation; bitcast merely preserves the same bits under another type.
explanation: The assignment highlights that integer 42 and double 42.0 have different bit patterns. A semantic cast must decode the source, numerically convert it, and encode the target.

The interpreter uses static_cast after std::bit_cast decoding. The compiler uses signed-integer-to-floating SIToFP and floating-to-signed-integer FPToSI. By contrast, the final DOUBLE result uses a bitcast only because it is being packed into the raw return ABI without changing its value.
pseudocode: INT64 -> DOUBLE: decode signed i64; numeric convert; encode double bits
DOUBLE -> INT64: decode double; truncate toward zero; encode signed i64 bits
same type: leave the payload/value unchanged
ABI packing: bitcast typed result without numeric conversion
invariants: A cast to the same type is an identity.
INT64 to DOUBLE treats the source as signed.
DOUBLE to INT64 is defined only for finite values whose truncated result is representable.
pitfalls: Implementing Cast with bitcast, so integer 42 becomes a tiny nonsensical double.
Using UIToFP rather than SIToFP for negative integers.
Ignoring NaN, infinity, and out-of-range FPToSI behavior.
Assuming the provided tests cover both cast directions and both execution paths.

source_refs.note: Explicitly requires a converting cast.
Interpreter numeric conversions.

concepts.title: Typed arithmetic and signed integer semantics
concepts.takeaway: LLVM arithmetic opcodes encode both the value domain and, for division, signedness.
explanation: Integer and floating addition, subtraction, and multiplication use separate opcode families: add/sub/mul versus fadd/fsub/fmul. Signed and unsigned integer add have the same low 64-bit result when no overflow flags are attached.

Division is different: the implementation correctly emits sdiv for signed INT64 and fdiv for DOUBLE. The interpreter decodes INT64 before C++ division. Neither path guards division by zero or INT64_MIN divided by -1.
pseudocode: before FPToSI: require finite, in-range input if defined behavior is needed
invariants: sdiv, not udiv, implements signed integer division.
Interpreter and compiler must choose operations from the same semantic type.
Overflow and exceptional inputs need an explicit shared policy if equivalence is required.
pitfalls: Using unsigned division because the transport carrier is uint64_t.
Calling signed C++ overflow equivalent to LLVM wrapping arithmetic; C++ signed overflow is undefined while plain LLVM add/sub/mul wrap modulo 2^64.
Relying on tests whose expected C++ expression itself overflows.
Assuming floating division by zero behaves like integer division by zero.

source_refs.note: C++ typed arithmetic and unguarded division.

Acknowledges that edge cases are not tested.

concepts.title: Module construction, optimization, lookup, and lifetime
concepts.takeaway: Compilation is a lifecycle: build valid IR, transfer module ownership to the JIT, resolve a symbol, then keep the JIT alive while calling it.
explanation: ExpressionCompiler creates one module in its constructor. compile declares compiled_expression, creates one entry block, recursively emits the root, returns its raw i64 payload, optionally prints IR, moves the module into the JIT, and stores the resolved machine-code pointer.

The ORC wrapper verifies and optimizes modules, compiles them for the host target, and owns executable memory until its execution session ends. In this submission, ExpressionCompiler is effectively one-shot because compile moves away its only module and always uses the same symbol name.
pseudocode: if root is DOUBLE: rawResult = bitcast typedResult to i64
verify; optimize; add module; lookup symbol; call while JIT lives
invariants: The LLVM context outlives the module/JIT operations that reference it.
A module is not used after ownership is moved into the JIT.
run is legal only after a successful non-null symbol lookup.
Generated function code remains valid only while the owning JIT session exists.
pitfalls: Calling compile twice on the same ExpressionCompiler: module is null after the first move and the symbol name is fixed.
Calling run before compile or after a failed lookup.
Printing verifier diagnostics but still adding an invalid module.
Destroying the compiler/JIT and retaining a stale function pointer.

source_refs.note: One-module compile and raw function-pointer lifecycle.

concepts.title: What the benchmark does—and does not—measure
concepts.takeaway: It compares repeated execution of one left-deep integer tree after compilation; it does not measure compile latency or general expression coverage.
explanation: The benchmark creates 1,000 Add/Sub/Mul nodes over 10, 100, or 1,000 arguments. The JIT path compiles once before the timed loop; both paths then evaluate the same fixed argument array repeatedly.

The result mainly exposes recursive virtual-dispatch and tree-walk overhead versus a straight-line optimized native function. It says nothing about DOUBLE, Cast, Div, branches, compilation amortization, changing inputs, or full query compilation.
pseudocode: setup: build left-deep tree; initialize fixed args
report items/sec separately; compilation cost excluded
invariants: The compared expression shape and inputs are identical.
Compilation time is outside the timed compiled loop.
The benchmark label must state its covered operations and tree shape.
pitfalls: Claiming the numbers include JIT startup cost.
Generalizing from integer Add/Sub/Mul to all expressions.
Ignoring that random large signed arithmetic likely overflows in the interpreter, where C++ signed overflow is undefined.
Treating a microbenchmark as end-to-end query-engine performance.

source_refs.note: Builds a left-deep INT64 Add/Sub/Mul tree.

trace.title: Follow a mixed DOUBLE-to-INT64 expression across the raw ABI
trace.setup: Use the test shape int64(((42.0 + a1) - (21.0 - a0))) + a2 + 100 with a0=2.5 encoded as DOUBLE bits, a1=-1.25 encoded as DOUBLE bits, and a2=7 encoded as INT64 bits.
steps: Argument nodes select slots by index and decode them by declared type; the slots themselves carry no runtime type tag.
Cast numerically converts 22.25 to signed INT64 22 by truncation toward zero. A bitcast here would be wrong.
The interpreter returns the raw bits of signed 129. The compiled function already has an i64 result and returns the same bits through data64_t.
trace.result: Both execution strategies should return the data64_t bit pattern for signed integer 129.

decisions.title: Use one eight-byte carrier for mixed scalar values
decisions.rationale: A uniform argument-array and function ABI makes JIT lookup and invocation simple while expression metadata preserves semantic types.
decisions.tradeoff: The ABI has no runtime tags, bounds, or NULL indicators; caller and expression tree must agree perfectly.

source_refs.note: Opaque carrier plus semantic ValueType.
Uniform i64-returning generated function.

decisions.title: Keep generated values typed inside LLVM
decisions.rationale: INT64 nodes produce i64 and DOUBLE nodes produce double, so LLVM can verify and optimize the expression using strongly typed SSA values.
decisions.tradeoff: The compiler must emit explicit numeric conversions at every type-changing Cast and pack DOUBLE only at the external ABI boundary.

source_refs.note: Typed constants, loads, conversions, and arithmetic.

decisions.title: Optimize through ORC before symbol lookup
decisions.rationale: Instruction combining, reassociation, GVN, and CFG simplification can fold constants and remove redundant work before host compilation.
decisions.tradeoff: Optimization adds compile latency and can expose undefined-semantics mismatches if the interpreter relies on C++ signed overflow.

source_refs.note: Configured function-level optimization passes.
Connects transform and compile layers.

decisions.title: Treat the compiler object as one-shot
decisions.rationale: The current implementation creates one module in the constructor and transfers it to the JIT on compile.
decisions.tradeoff: A second compile dereferences a moved-away module and would also reuse the fixed compiled_expression symbol; reusable compilation requires a fresh module and symbol/resource policy.

drills.prompt: Read a supplied straight-line LLVM function, rewrite its SSA definitions as one arithmetic expression, substitute known globals, and constant-fold the result.
drills.answer: Start at ret and recursively substitute each SSA definition. Respect opcode types and signedness. Replace compile-time-known globals, evaluate constant arithmetic and comparisons, select the surviving branch, then remove dead definitions and unreachable blocks.
checklist: Follow SSA use-def chains from the return value.
Track each value's LLVM type.
Distinguish sdiv/udiv and signed/unsigned comparisons.
Substitute only values explicitly known at compile time.
Remove dead code only after proving it cannot affect the result.

drills.prompt: Explain why casting integer 42 to DOUBLE must not use a bitcast.
drills.answer: The raw bits for integer 42 represent a tiny unrelated double. Numeric cast SIToFP computes double 42.0 with its own IEEE bit pattern; bitcast is appropriate only when packing or unpacking an already-computed value across the raw data64_t ABI.
checklist: Name the two distinct bit patterns.
Use SIToFP for signed INT64 to DOUBLE.
Use FPToSI for DOUBLE to signed INT64.
Reserve bitcast for representation transport.

drills.prompt: Debug an implementation that emits udiv for every INT64 division.
drills.answer: The expression type is signed INT64 even though data64_t is uint64_t. Decode/interpret the payload as signed and emit sdiv. A direct case such as -7/2 should produce -3 with truncation toward zero.
checklist: Do not infer semantic signedness from the transport type.
Use a negative direct test.
Mention division-by-zero and INT64_MIN/-1.
Keep interpreter and compiled policies aligned.

drills.prompt: Sketch the LLVM wrapper function for a DOUBLE root and explain every conversion.
drills.answer: Declare i64 @compiled_expression(ptr args), recursively build a typed double result, bitcast that double to i64 without changing bits, and ret i64. Typed child Cast nodes still use numeric conversion instructions.
checklist: Use a uniform raw external ABI.
Load each Argument using its semantic type.
Bitcast only the final DOUBLE result for transport.
Keep the JIT alive while calling the resolved address.

drills.prompt: What conclusion can and cannot be drawn from the provided interpreter-versus-compiled benchmark?
drills.answer: It compares steady-state calls for one 1,000-node left-deep INT64 Add/Sub/Mul tree after JIT compilation. It can show virtual tree-walk overhead versus optimized straight-line code, but excludes compilation cost and does not cover casts, division, doubles, branches, changing inputs, or end-to-end queries.
checklist: State that compile time is outside the timed loop.
Name the exact operations and tree shape.
Note that inputs are fixed during timing.
Flag signed-overflow undefined behavior in the interpreted workload.

lecture_links.note: Motivation for native compilation; LLVM typed SSA and phi nodes; direct scalar-expression lowering; and the larger goal of retaining values in registers inside data-centric pipelines.

limitations: The project has no accompanying student report; all conclusions come from README, code, tests, benchmark, JIT wrapper, examples, and lecture evidence.
The current host lacks cmake and an LLVM 21 development installation, so the 29 provided tests and benchmark were not executed in this audit.
Constant constructors and many tests decode/encode via reinterpret_cast lvalue dereferences; std::bit_cast or memcpy is safer under C++ aliasing rules.
Interpreter INT64 add/sub/mul use signed C++ arithmetic, where overflow is undefined, while plain LLVM integer arithmetic wraps modulo 2^64; equivalence is not defined on overflow.
Integer division by zero and INT64_MIN/-1 are unguarded; DOUBLE-to-INT64 conversion of NaN, infinity, or out-of-range values is also undefined/poison territory.
Argument lookup has no runtime argument count, bounds check, type tag, NULL flag, or alignment check.
Expression nodes hold child references rather than ownership, so child lifetimes must exceed parent evaluation or compilation.
ExpressionCompiler is effectively one-shot, does not guard run-before-compile, and does not reject a null symbol pointer.
JIT::addModule prints invalid-module diagnostics but still forwards the module to the optimization/compile layer.
The benchmark excludes compilation cost, covers only INT64 Add/Sub/Mul in a left-deep tree, uses fixed inputs, and likely invokes signed-overflow undefined behavior in the interpreter.

high_priority_findings.title: Interpreter/compiler overflow mismatch
high_priority_findings.detail: C++ signed overflow is undefined; emitted LLVM add/sub/mul without nsw/nuw wrap. Random complex tests and benchmark use values that make overflow likely.

high_priority_findings.title: Provided constant test is tautological
high_priority_findings.detail: InterpretedIntegerConstant compares result with itself and cannot detect a wrong implementation.

high_priority_findings.title: Cast coverage is one-sided
high_priority_findings.detail: Only compiled DOUBLE-to-INT64 is tested; interpreter Cast and INT64-to-DOUBLE are uncovered.

high_priority_findings.title: Compilation lifecycle lacks defensive checks
high_priority_findings.detail: The module is moved on first compile, fnPtr may remain null, run calls it unconditionally, and verifier failure does not reject the module.
